title: Raga Dhanasri
hook: a raga of true wealth that opens with a frightened soul

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Sorath: Guru Tegh Bahadur's level person, blending with God like water with water. Your line was calm in sorath. When praise or criticism came, did it pass? Day one thousand eighty-four.

Who counts as rich? A bank would answer with a number. A grandmother might answer with the people at her table. Today's raga has its own answer, and it arrives in a strange order. Tradition links Raga Dhanasri with contentment and true wealth. So you might expect its first hymn to sound settled and full. Instead, the first voice you hear in Dhanasri is afraid. Today: Raga Dhanasri, and how a raga of true wealth starts from fear.
screen: `WHO COUNTS AS RICH?` → `A RAGA OF TRUE WEALTH.` → `ITS FIRST VOICE IS AFRAID.`

segments.voice: Dhanasri comes after Sorath in the Granth's order. Its first hymn is Guru Nanak's, and it begins, jeeo darat hai aapna. In paraphrase: my soul is afraid; to whom should I cry out? Then the hymn answers its own question. I serve the one who makes pain forgotten, the giver who is always, always giving. That's the first move. The hymn doesn't pretend the fear isn't there. It names it, then turns toward a giver who never runs out. Now hold that next to the raga's name. Further into Dhanasri, a hymn of Guru Amar Das plays on it. In paraphrase: Dhanasri is known as truly wealthy when she does the True Guru's work, when she gives over body and mind to that service. Dhanvanti, the wealthy one, chimes with Dhanasri, and the Guru lets the two words ring together. Some readers hear the soul as a bride in her, and if so, the bride's riches aren't jewelry. They're the work she does. Put the two hymns side by side and you get today's idea in two steps. Fear first, honestly said: I don't have enough, I can't hold this. Then a different kind of wealth: a giver who keeps giving, and a life spent in service. True wealth, in Dhanasri, isn't what you keep. It's what you're held by, and what you give. Contentment follows from that, because a person held by an endless giver can stop counting. Today's line: true wealth.
screen: `FIRST VOICE: MY SOUL IS AFRAID.` · `THE GIVER WHO IS ALWAYS GIVING.` · `DHANASRI, DHANVANTI: THE WEALTHY ONE.` · `RICHES THAT ARE SERVICE.` · then, large: `TRUE WEALTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to Dhanasri, and take an honest count. If you can, play a shabad sung in Raga Dhanasri. Then sit. First, let one worry about not having enough come up: money, time, strength, patience. Name it plainly, the way the hymn does. Then, slowly, count what's holding you right now that you didn't earn: breath, a floor, someone who would pick up if you called. Let the count go on for as long as it goes. If you pray, you can say Waheguru after each thing you count. If you don't, simply keep counting. The bell holds the time.
Raga Dhanasri. The raga after Sorath, linked by tradition with contentment and true wealth, which opens with a frightened soul and finds riches in service. Today's word.
Your line: true wealth. Today, spend something that doesn't come from your wallet: ten minutes of real help, given to someone who can't pay you back. Day one thousand eighty-four.

howItsDone: Ragis sing shabads from the Dhanasri section of the Guru Granth Sahib in Raga Dhanasri during kirtan, and the raga's opening hymn by Guru Nanak is sung in gurdwaras as well as read.

notes: Both hymns are paraphrased. Please confirm that 'Jeeo darat hai aapna kai sio kari pukaar / dookh visaaran seviaa sada sada daataar' is the opening hymn of Dhanasri (Ang 660).

Please confirm the author and Ang of 'Dhanasri dhanvanti janiai bhai jaa satgur ki kaar kamaae' (given here as Guru Amar Das, Ang 666) and that the paraphrase (truly wealthy when she does the True Guru's work, giving over body and mind) is fair.
The script says the hymn lets Dhanasri and dhanvanti 'ring together'; it makes no claim about the raga name's origin.
Contentment and true wealth as the raga's mood are from the outline and presented as tradition.
Original: ਧਨਾਸਰੀ; please confirm spelling and pronunciation.
The outline's word for this day is the title head ('Raga Dhanasri'), kept exactly.
Editor pass: the soul-as-bride reading is now attributed to 'some readers' rather than stated as the hymn's own frame.
